# Introduction

Earlier this year, a very interesting research article came out from a team at
Meta. In this [paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.09871), they propose a new transformers-based architecture for LLMs
which operates at the level of _bytes_ rather than at the level of _tokens_,
thus being dubbed the _Byte Latent Transformer_ (BLT for short 🥪). One
of the central motivations for their proposal is that current tokenization-based
approaches to LLMs are inefficient, in as far as tokenization is a pre-computed
grouping of bytes which doesn't necessarily allocate compute resources
intelligently based on the context. To justify their new architecture, they show
the results from several experiments which shows that their model performs as
well as (or even better in some instances) other frontier models. My goals for
this post is:

* Explain in greater detail the motivation to work on bytes
* Explain the model architecture and how training and inference work.
* Discuss the empirical studies done by the authors as the relate to performance
  and scaling laws for their architecture.
* Raise some questions that I had from reading the paper. 

This post is by no means a substitute for reading the paper, and I highly
encourage you to go do so. However, I hope this post helps in some small way.
And of course, it should go without saying, that any mistakes are mine and mine
alone, and feel free to email me if you have any corrections. 

# LLMs and Tokenization

Before getting into the nitty-gritty of the BLT architecture it seems best to
remind ourselves how LLMs currently work and where this brings up bottlenecks
and pitfalls. <!-- Not sure I love this phrasing -->  Of main concern for the
BLT paper, in particular, is the reliance on tokenization for LLMs. Below is a
diagram which caricatures how LLMs currently work. 

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[Input String] --> B[Tokenizer]
  B --> C[Sequence of Tokens]
  C --> D[Decoder-only Transformer]
  D --> E[Probability Distribution]
  E --> F[Next Token]
```
